claim: Half of all anticancer drugs developed since the 1940s are natural products or derivatives of natural products.
source: Natural products are an important source for the development of pharmaceutical drugs, especially in oncology; half of all anticancer drugs developed since the 1940s are natural products or derivatives of natural products (Newman and Cragg, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Newman and Cragg, 2012.

claim: Ophiobolin A (OPA) is a plant toxin isolated from pathogenic fungi of the Bipolaris genus.
source: An example of such a natural product is ophiobolin A (OPA), a plant toxin isolated from pathogenic fungi of the Bipolaris genus which displays cytotoxicity at nanomolar concentrations against a range of cancer cell lines (Au et al., 2000; Bury et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Au et al., 2000 and Bury et al., 2013.

claim: OPA displays cytotoxicity at nanomolar concentrations against a range of cancer cell lines.
source: An example of such a natural product is ophiobolin A (OPA), a plant toxin isolated from pathogenic fungi of the Bipolaris genus which displays cytotoxicity at nanomolar concentrations against a range of cancer cell lines (Au et al., 2000; Bury et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Au et al., 2000 and Bury et al., 2013.

claim: OPA induces paraptosis, a form of non-apoptotic cell death, in glioblastoma cells.
source: OPA induces paraptosis, a form of non-apoptotic cell death, in glioblastoma cells and displays antitumor activity in a mouse glioblastoma model (Bury et al., 2013; Dasari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bury et al., 2013 and Dasari et al., 2015.

claim: OPA displays antitumor activity in a mouse glioblastoma model.
source: OPA induces paraptosis, a form of non-apoptotic cell death, in glioblastoma cells and displays antitumor activity in a mouse glioblastoma model (Bury et al., 2013; Dasari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bury et al., 2013 and Dasari et al., 2015.

claim: The toxicity of OPA to plants is believed to involve calmodulin inhibition via formation of a covalent adduct between OPA and specific lysine side chains.
source: The toxicity of OPA to plants is believed to involve calmodulin inhibition via formation of a covalent adduct between OPA and specific lysine side chains (Leung et al., 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Leung et al., 1984.

claim: Primary amines react with the 1,4-dicarbonyl moiety of OPA to form covalent adducts.
source: More recently, it has been shown in synthetic studies that primary amines react with the 1,4-dicarbonyl moiety of OPA to form covalent adducts and that this moiety is critical for animal cell cytotoxicity, leading the authors to suggest that the MOA of OPA in animal cells is through covalent modification of an unknown intracellular target protein (Dasari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dasari et al., 2015.

claim: The 1,4-dicarbonyl moiety of OPA is critical for animal cell cytotoxicity.
source: More recently, it has been shown in synthetic studies that primary amines react with the 1,4-dicarbonyl moiety of OPA to form covalent adducts and that this moiety is critical for animal cell cytotoxicity, leading the authors to suggest that the MOA of OPA in animal cells is through covalent modification of an unknown intracellular target protein (Dasari et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dasari et al., 2015.

claim: Genetic inactivation of de novo synthesis of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) mitigates OPA cytotoxicity by reducing cellular PE levels.
source: We found that genetic inactivation of de novo synthesis of phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) mitigates OPA cytotoxicity by reducing cellular PE levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including genetic screens and PE quantification experiments.

claim: OPA reacts with the ethanolamine head group of PE in human cells to form pyrrole-containing covalent cytotoxic adducts.
source: OPA reacts with the ethanolamine head group of PE in human cells to form pyrrole-containing covalent cytotoxic adducts and these adducts lead to lipid bilayer destabilization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data including LC-MS/MS analysis and PLD digestion experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: PE-OPA adducts lead to lipid bilayer destabilization.
source: OPA reacts with the ethanolamine head group of PE in human cells to form pyrrole-containing covalent cytotoxic adducts and these adducts lead to lipid bilayer destabilization.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from liposome leakage assays shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Three genes (ETNK1, PCYT2, and EPT1) had a significant enrichment of retroviral insertions in the OPA resistance screen.
source: Three genes had a significant enrichment of retroviral insertions: ethanolamine kinase 1 (ETNK1, p = 7.2 × 10−12), phosphate cytidylyltransferase 2, ethanolamine (PCYT2, p = 4.0 × 10−7), and ethanolaminephosphotransferase 1 (EPT1, p = 4.0 × 10−7) (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the genetic screen shown in Figure 1a with specific p-values provided.

claim: ETNK1, PCYT2, and EPT1 encode the three enzymes required for the de novo synthesis of PE, also known as the Kennedy pathway.
source: These three genes encode the three enzymes required for the de novo synthesis of PE, also known as the Kennedy pathway (Gibellini and Smith, 2010) (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gibellini and Smith, 2010 and illustrated in Figure 1b.

claim: PCYT2GT and ETNK1GT cell lines showed reduced PE levels compared to KBM7 cells, by 24% and 16%, respectively.
source: Both PCYT2GT and ETNK1GT cell lines showed reduced PE levels compared to KBM7 cells, by 24% and 16%, respectively (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from phospholipid quantification shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Expression of PCYT2 in PCYT2GT cells restores OPA sensitivity.
source: To validate that inactivation of the Kennedy pathway causes OPA resistance, we transduced PCYT2GT cells with a lentiviral construct driving expression of PCYT2 and observed that this complementation rescues OPA sensitivity (Figure 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from complementation experiments shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Silencing PCYT2 in HEK293T cells leads to increased OPA resistance.
source: Cells expressing two shRNA (short hairpin RNA) constructs had 85% and 70% reduced PCYT2 mRNA levels, respectively (Figure 2a), exhibited increased OPA resistance (Figure 2b), and had reduced cellular PE levels (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from shRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2a-c.

claim: OPA treatment activates the Kennedy pathway and increases PE content in HEK293T and HCT116 cells.
source: Interestingly, when either cell line was treated with concentrations of OPA that induced mild cytotoxicity, both the average flux through the Kennedy pathway (measured by accumulation of the radiolabel into PE) and the steady state level of PE were increased compared to vehicle-treated cells (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radiolabeled ethanolamine incorporation assays shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Addition of exogenous PE to cells treated with OPA rescues cell viability.
source: In agreement with this prediction, addition of a commercial preparation of PE to cells treated with a cytotoxic amount of OPA rescued cell viability, whereas addition of the phospholipids phosphatidylcholine (PC) or phosphatidylserine (PS) had no effect (Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Ethanolamine and O-phosphorylethanolamine can inactivate OPA, although much less potently than PE.
source: In addition, we observed that constituents of the head group of PE, ethanolamine and O-phosphorylethanolamine, could inactivate OPA, although much less potently than PE, and that triethanolamine (lacking a primary amine) had no effect (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from OPA inactivation assays shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Triethanolamine (lacking a primary amine) has no effect on OPA inactivation.
source: In addition, we observed that constituents of the head group of PE, ethanolamine and O-phosphorylethanolamine, could inactivate OPA, although much less potently than PE, and that triethanolamine (lacking a primary amine) had no effect (Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from OPA inactivation assays shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Incubation of OPA with an excess of ethanolamine abolishes cytotoxicity.
source: Incubation of OPA with an excess of ethanolamine abolished cytotoxicity and analysis by LC-MS/MS revealed that the main product of this reaction is consistent with formation of a covalent adduct with two dehydration reactions (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays and LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: The main product of the reaction between OPA and ethanolamine is consistent with formation of a covalent adduct with two dehydration reactions.
source: Incubation of OPA with an excess of ethanolamine abolished cytotoxicity and analysis by LC-MS/MS revealed that the main product of this reaction is consistent with formation of a covalent adduct with two dehydration reactions (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Incubation of the reaction product of OPA and ethanolamine with Ehrlich's reagent yields a purple solution characteristic of pyrroles.
source: Incubation of the reaction product of OPA and ethanolamine with Ehrlich's reagent (Amarnath et al., 2004) yielded a purple solution (Amax = 580 nm), characteristic of pyrroles (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Ehrlich's test shown in Figure 3e and a citation to Amarnath et al., 2004.

claim: OPA forms a pyrrole-containing covalent adduct with PE which can be hydrolyzed by phospholipase D to release ethanolamine-OPA (Etn-OPA).
source: The detection of Etn-OPA was dependent on the presence of PE and OPA, and PLD treatment, demonstrating that OPA forms a pyrrole-containing covalent adduct with PE which PLD is able to hydrolyze into Etn-OPA (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro reactions and LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: PE-OPA adducts are present in lipids extracted from HEK293T and HCT116 cells treated with OPA.
source: The quenched extracted phospholipids were digested with PLD and analyzed by LC-MS/MS, which revealed the presence of Etn-OPA dependent on OPA and PLD treatment (Figure 4c–d and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from LC-MS/MS analysis of cellular lipid extracts shown in Figure 4c-d and supplementary figures.

claim: OPA does not react with cellular ethanolamine.
source: Importantly, the absence of Etn-OPA in the control lacking PLD treatment indicates that OPA does not react with cellular ethanolamine (Figure 4c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: OPA treatment causes extensive liposome leakage, and the extent of leakage is directly dependent on both the PE content of the liposomes and on the OPA concentration.
source: We observed that OPA treatment caused extensive liposome leakage, and that the extent of leakage is directly dependent on both the PE content of the liposomes and on the OPA concentration (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from liposome leakage assays shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Liposomes composed only of PC or with very low PE content remain intact even at high OPA concentration.
source: Importantly, we observed that liposomes composed only of PC or with very low PE content remain intact even at high OPA concentration, indicating that the leakage is likely specifically due to the formation of PE-OPA adducts.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from liposome leakage assays shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Loss-of-function genetic screens in KBM7 cells can robustly identify genes involved in the cytotoxicity of anticancer drugs with well-characterized MOAs.
source: As expected, we observed enrichment of inactivating insertions in genes known to play a role in the MOA of these anticancer compounds (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens with multiple anticancer drugs shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Doxorubicin and etoposide induce cytotoxicity by forming a ternary complex with DNA and the enzyme topoisomerase IIA.
source: For instance, doxorubicin and etoposide induce cytotoxicity by forming a ternary complex with DNA and the enzyme topoisomerase IIA (Pommier et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pommier et al., 2010.

claim: In screens with doxorubicin and etoposide, there was a significant enrichment of inactivating insertions in gene TOP2A, which encodes topoisomerase IIA.
source: In both screens, we detected a significant enrichment of inactivating insertions in gene TOP2A, which encodes topoisomerase IIA (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a-b.

claim: Bortezomib kills cancer cells by proteasome inhibition.
source: Bortezomib kills cancer cells by proteasome inhibition (Adams, 2004) and, accordingly, we observed a significant enrichment of inactivating insertions in genes encoding proteasome subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Adams, 2004.

claim: In the bortezomib screen, there was a significant enrichment of inactivating insertions in genes encoding proteasome subunits.
source: Bortezomib kills cancer cells by proteasome inhibition (Adams, 2004) and, accordingly, we observed a significant enrichment of inactivating insertions in genes encoding proteasome subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from genetic screens shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2d.

claim: At least one gene in the Kennedy pathway was enriched above background at every OPA concentration tested.
source: To test the robustness of this result, we repeated screens at different concentrations of OPA; at least one gene in the Kennedy pathway was enriched above background at every concentration tested (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from multiple genetic screens shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: PCYT2GT and ETNK1GT cell lines had strongly reduced levels (<2%) of either PCYT2 or ETNK1 mRNA, as quantified by RT-qPCR.
source: As expected, these cell lines had strongly reduced levels (<2%) of either PCYT2 or ETNK1 mRNA, as quantified by RT-qPCR (Figure 1c)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from RT-qPCR shown in Figure 1c.

claim: PCYT2GT and ETNK1GT clones were less sensitive to OPA than wild-type KBM7 cells.
source: As expected, these cell lines had strongly reduced levels (<2%) of either PCYT2 or ETNK1 mRNA, as quantified by RT-qPCR (Figure 1c) and, consistent with the screening results, both clones were less sensitive to OPA (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from cell viability assays shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 4a.

claim: Human cells can synthesize PE through multiple mechanisms, the two major ones being the Kennedy pathway and decarboxylation of phosphatidylserine in mitochondria.
source: Since human cells can synthesize PE through multiple mechanisms (the two major ones being the Kennedy pathway and decarboxylation of phosphatidylserine in mitochondria; Gibellini and Smith, 2010), and it is known that cells employ mechanisms to maintain homeostasis of phospholipid levels (Hermansson et al., 2011), we tested whether inactivation of the Kennedy pathway in KBM7 cells decreases total cellular PE levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gibellini and Smith, 2010 and Hermansson et al., 2011.

claim: Cells employ mechanisms to maintain homeostasis of phospholipid levels.
source: Since human cells can synthesize PE through multiple mechanisms (the two major ones being the Kennedy pathway and decarboxylation of phosphatidylserine in mitochondria; Gibellini and Smith, 2010), and it is known that cells employ mechanisms to maintain homeostasis of phospholipid levels (Hermansson et al., 2011), we tested whether inactivation of the Kennedy pathway in KBM7 cells decreases total cellular PE levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hermansson et al., 2011.

claim: Meclizine directly inhibits PCYT2, reducing the average flux through the Kennedy pathway.
source: There is precedent for small molecules that target the Kennedy pathway: the antihistamine and antiemetic drug meclizine directly inhibits PCYT2, reducing the average flux through the Kennedy pathway (Gohil et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gohil et al., 2013.

claim: Treatment with meclizine decreases the flux through the Kennedy pathway and reduces PE content.
source: In contrast, when we treated cells with meclizine we observed the expected decrease in the flux through the pathway and reduced PE content (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from radiolabeled ethanolamine incorporation assays shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The concentration of PE required to inactivate OPA in vitro is at least 2000-fold lower than that of ethanolamine or lysine.
source: While we cannot exclude the possibility that covalent modification of cellular proteins contributes to the observed toxicity of OPA, our experimental results show that the concentration of PE required to inactivate OPA in vitro is at least 2000-fold lower than that of ethanolamine or lysine (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from OPA inactivation assays shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A mild reduction in PE levels (16–24%) was accompanied by a mild increase in OPA resistance (IC50 from 43 nM in wild-type cells to 70–85 nM in the mutants).
source: Accordingly, we observed that a mild reduction in PE levels (16–24%) was accompanied by a mild increase in OPA resistance (IC50 from 43 nM in wild-type cells to 70–85 nM in the mutants) (Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from PE quantification and cell viability assays shown in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 4a.

claim: The C-6 epimer of OPA (6-epi-OPA) is 40-fold less cytotoxic than OPA.
source: Notably, the C-6 epimer of OPA (6-epi-OPA) is 40-fold less cytotoxic than OPA (Dasari et al., 2015), although both compounds would form the same pyrrole adduct upon reaction with PE, as the stereocenter at position 6 is lost with pyrrole formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dasari et al., 2015.

claim: Both OPA and 6-epi-OPA would form the same pyrrole adduct upon reaction with PE, as the stereocenter at position 6 is lost with pyrrole formation.
source: Notably, the C-6 epimer of OPA (6-epi-OPA) is 40-fold less cytotoxic than OPA (Dasari et al., 2015), although both compounds would form the same pyrrole adduct upon reaction with PE, as the stereocenter at position 6 is lost with pyrrole formation.
evidence: The claim is based on chemical reasoning about the structure of the pyrrole adduct.

claim: The ring cyclization step is the rate limiting step of the Paal-Knorr reaction.
source: The ring cyclization step is the rate limiting step of the Paal-Knorr reaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and this step is strongly influenced by the stereochemistry of the 1,4 diketone; rates of pyrrole formation can be up to 57-fold different between stereoisomers (Amarnath et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Amarnath et al., 1991.

claim: Rates of pyrrole formation can be up to 57-fold different between stereoisomers of 1,4-diketones.
source: The ring cyclization step is the rate limiting step of the Paal-Knorr reaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and this step is strongly influenced by the stereochemistry of the 1,4 diketone; rates of pyrrole formation can be up to 57-fold different between stereoisomers (Amarnath et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Amarnath et al., 1991.

claim: Polygodial, a 1,4-dialdehyde antifungal compound, forms a pyrrole-containing adduct with PE on the cell surface that is directly linked to its antifungal activity.
source: Cytotoxicity through modification of PE has previously been reported for polygodial, a 1,4-dialdehyde antifungal compound, which has been shown to form a pyrrole-containing adduct with PE on the cell surface that is directly linked to its antifungal activity (Fujita and Kubo, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fujita and Kubo, 2005.

claim: Covalent modification of PE with isoketals alters membrane curvature because the newly formed bulky hydrophobic head group partitions to the lipid bilayer and increases lateral pressure.
source: Furthermore, it has been previously shown that covalent modification of PE with isoketals alters membrane curvature because the newly formed bulky hydrophobic head group partitions to the lipid bilayer and increases lateral pressure (Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2011.

claim: PE is ubiquitously found in nature.
source: Considering our work in human cells and the fact that PE is ubiquitously found in nature (Vance and Tasseva, 2013), PE may be the main target of OPA in plants and potentially other organisms.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vance and Tasseva, 2013.

claim: PE is found in higher quantities on the outer leaflet of cancer cells.
source: Indeed, it has recently been shown that PE is found in higher quantities on the outer leaflet of cancer cells (Stafford and Thorpe, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Stafford and Thorpe, 2011.

claim: Host defense peptides display selectivity against cancer cells based on the difference in surface phospholipid composition compared to normal cells.
source: Furthermore, host defense peptides have been shown to display selectively against cancer cells based on the difference in surface phospholipid composition compared to normal cells (Leite et al., 2015; Riedl et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Leite et al., 2015 and Riedl et al., 2011.

claim: OPA is cytotoxic towards a broad range of organisms.
source: In addition to its activity in human cells, OPA is cytotoxic towards a broad range of organisms (Au et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Au et al., 2000.

claim: Early studies on the mechanism of cytotoxicity of OPA in plant cells suggested that it causes non-specific damage to membranes.
source: Early studies on the mechanism of cytotoxicity of OPA in plant cells suggested that it causes non-specific damage to membranes (Chattopadhyay and Samaddar, 1976) or even "covalent modification of some membrane component" (Tipton et al., 1977).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chattopadhyay and Samaddar, 1976 and Tipton et al., 1977.

claim: The selective antitumor activity displayed by OPA may be due to altered membrane PE levels in cancer cells.
source: Our characterization of this unusual cytotoxicity mechanism, made possible by unbiased genetic screening in human cells, suggests that the selective antitumor activity displayed by OPA may be due to altered membrane PE levels in cancer cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings and cited literature about PE distribution in cancer cells.

claim: PE represents the main target of OPA in human cells.
source: As the amplitude of changes in the observed cytotoxicity of OPA can be accounted for by changes in PE levels, we believe that PE represents the main target of OPA in human cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing correlation between PE levels and OPA cytotoxicity.

claim: Formation of PE-OPA adducts disrupts the lipid bilayer of human cells to induce cell death.
source: We hypothesize that formation of PE-OPA adducts disrupts the lipid bilayer of human cells to induce cell death.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the liposome leakage experiments shown in Figure 5a.

claim: OPA might display higher potency against cells or tissues containing high PE contents.
source: Interestingly, this observation is consistent with our expectation that the rate of adduct formation is dependent on PE content and suggests that OPA might display higher potency against cells or tissues containing high PE contents.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed dependence of membrane leakage on PE content.

claim: The activation of the Kennedy pathway seen upon OPA treatment may be a cellular response to the formation of PE-OPA adducts due to mechanisms regulating membrane PE homeostasis.
source: The activation of the pathway seen upon OPA treatment may be a cellular response to the formation of PE-OPA adducts due to mechanisms regulating membrane PE homeostasis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed activation of the Kennedy pathway upon OPA treatment.

claim: PE may be the main target of OPA in plants and potentially other organisms.
source: Considering our work in human cells and the fact that PE is ubiquitously found in nature (Vance and Tasseva, 2013), PE may be the main target of OPA in plants and potentially other organisms.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings in human cells and the ubiquity of PE.

claim: The selectivity of OPA for PE over ethanolamine, lysine, or other abundant primary amines may arise because OPA accumulates in lipid aggregates and efficiently reacts with PE due to high local concentrations or the hydrophobic environment.
source: This selectivity may arise because, at the concentrations tested, ethanolamine and lysine are freely soluble in aqueous buffers whereas PE forms insoluble lipid aggregates. Considering the lipophilic nature of OPA, it is likely that OPA accumulates in the lipid aggregates and efficiently reacts with PE due to high local concentrations or to the hydrophobic environment, or both.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed selectivity of OPA for PE.

claim: The 40-fold difference in potency between OPA and 6-epi-OPA can likely be attributed to differences in the rate of pyrrole adduct formation.
source: Thus, the 40-fold difference in potency between OPA and 6-epi-OPA can likely be attributed to differences in the rate of pyrrole adduct formation, and this observation supports our model that cytotoxicity depends on the amount of PE-OPA adduct formed.
evidence: This is an inference based on known chemistry of Paal-Knorr reactions and the observed difference in cytotoxicity.

claim: The extent of lipid bilayer destabilization is highest in the plasma membrane as it is the first source of PE encountered by OPA.
source: We believe such a mechanism may contribute to the ability of PE-OPA adducts to disrupt lipid bilayers, and suspect that the extent of lipid bilayer destabilization is highest in the plasma membrane as it is the first source of PE encountered by OPA.
evidence: This is a speculation about where OPA-induced membrane damage occurs.

claim: This is the first study to uncover a non-protein based target using genetic tools in human cells.
source: Few studies have yet taken advantage of the recent development of novel genetic tools in human cells to identify the target of small molecules, and this is the first study to uncover a non-protein based target (Nijman, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nijman, 2015 and the novelty of the findings.

claim: Insertional mutagenesis in haploid cells and CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing have revolutionized the use of genetic screens in human cell lines to facilitate the study of the MOA of bioactive molecules.
source: Recent technical breakthroughs, such as insertional mutagenesis in haploid cells (Carette et al., 2009, 2011) and CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing (Wang et al., 2014; Shalem et al., 2014; Gilbert et al., 2014; Smurnyy et al., 2014) have revolutionized the use of genetic screens in human cell lines to facilitate the study of the MOA of bioactive molecules in model systems more relevant to human disease (Nijman, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: Loss-of-function genetic screens in human KBM7 cells have been used to identify cellular factors that are necessary for entry of viruses and bacterial toxins, and transporters of small molecules.
source: Loss-of-function genetic screens in human KBM7 cells have been used to identify cellular factors that are necessary for entry of viruses and bacterial toxins, and transporters of small molecules, but rarely to identify the molecular targets of small molecule drugs (Carette et al., 2011; Nijman, 2015; Winter et al., 2014; Reiling et al., 2011; Birsoy et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to relevant literature.

claim: The mutagenized KBM7 library covers more than 95% of all expressed genes.
source: Briefly, we used a retroviral gene-trap approach to generate approximately 75 million insertions in the near-haploid human cell line KBM7, covering more than 95% of all expressed genes (Carette et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carette et al., 2011.

claim: Insertions in exonic regions or in the sense orientation of intronic regions are typically expected to cause gene inactivation.
source: Insertions in exonic regions or in the sense orientation of intronic regions are typically expected to cause gene inactivation (Carette et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carette et al., 2009.

claim: Overexpression of ABCG2 causes resistance to topotecan.
source: It is known that overexpression, not inactivation, of this transporter causes resistance to topotecan (Mao and Unadkat, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mao and Unadkat, 2015.

claim: Deficiency of DCK is associated with gemcitabine resistance.
source: Deficiency of DCK is associated with gemcitabine resistance (Bergman et al., 2002)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bergman et al., 2002.

claim: CDADC1 is a cytidine and dCMP deaminase known to be involved in resistance to deoxycytidine analogs.
source: CDADC1 is a cytidine and dCMP deaminase known to be involved in resistance to deoxycytidine analogs (Cai et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cai et al., 2008.

claim: SLC43A2 is a solute carrier that transports neutral amino acids into cells.
source: The screen with oxaliplatin, a DNA crosslinker, identified SLC43A2, a solute carrier that transports neutral amino acids into cells (Bodoy et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bodoy et al., 2013.

claim: Solute carriers play a role in the transport of anticancer drugs.
source: suggesting that SLC43A2 facilitates the transport of oxaliplatin into cells consistent with the known role of solute carriers in the transport of anticancer drugs (Li and Shu, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li and Shu, 2014.
